title: The Walls of Jericho Fall
summary: The LORD tells Joshua that Jericho is already given into his hand and commands an unusual strategy: for six days the army and seven priests blowing rams' horns march once around the city with the ark, and on the seventh day they circle it seven times. At the long blast of the horns the people shout, the wall collapses, and Israel takes the city. Jericho is devoted to the LORD for destruction, its precious metals go to the LORD's treasury, and Rahab and her family are spared. Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds the city.
story: Israel is camped at Gilgal, circumcised, having kept the Passover, and Joshua has just bowed before the commander of the LORD's army. Now the LORD speaks the battle plan, and it is not a military one. Jericho, the first city in the land, becomes a demonstration that the land is God's gift, taken by obedience and worship rather than by siege craft. The chapter also brings Rahab's story to its promised end, as the spies keep their oath. At the same time it introduces the ban, the devoting of the city to God, which will become the test Israel fails in chapter 7 when Achan secretly takes what was devoted.
historical:
Jericho (Tell es-Sultan) guarded the eastern approach to the central hill country. The archaeology of the site in the Late Bronze Age is one of the most debated questions in biblical archaeology. John Garstang, excavating in the 1930s, identified a collapsed wall and a destruction layer he dated to around 1400 BC. Kathleen Kenyon, excavating in the 1950s with more refined methods, redated that destruction to around 1550 BC and concluded that the city was small or unoccupied in the period usually proposed for Joshua, and that the collapsed wall Garstang found was much older. In 1990 Bryant Wood reexamined the pottery and argued for a destruction around 1400 BC, a proposal that others have disputed. Heavy erosion of the mound over the centuries complicates every reconstruction. Readers who hold different views on the date of the conquest and on the nature of the text interpret this evidence differently, and the question remains open.

The curse in verse 26 found its fulfillment, according to 1 Kings 16:34, in the days of King Ahab in the ninth century BC, when Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho at the cost of his firstborn and youngest sons. The site was not entirely abandoned in between (Judges 3:13 and 2 Samuel 10:5 mention the city of palms and Jericho), so the curse seems to have concerned rebuilding it as a fortified city with foundations and gates.
cultural:
The ram's horn (shofar) was not a musical instrument in the modern sense but a signal horn, used to summon people, sound alarms, and announce holy occasions such as the Day of Atonement in the Year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25:9). The procession around Jericho looks more like a liturgy than a siege: priests, horns, the ark, silence, and a climactic shout. The number seven (seven priests, seven horns, seven days, seven circuits on the seventh day) marks the event as sacred and complete, echoing the seven days of creation.

The ban (herem) was an ancient Near Eastern practice in which a city and its people were devoted wholly to a deity, meaning that its inhabitants were killed and its goods destroyed or given to the god's sanctuary, with no plunder for the victors. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription from the ninth century BC, uses the same term when King Mesha boasts of devoting the Israelite town of Nebo to his god. In Israel the ban was understood as giving to the LORD what belonged to him and removing what would lead the people into idolatry (Deuteronomy 7:1-6, 20:16-18). It is important to note that it did not permit personal gain: Israel's soldiers were forbidden to enrich themselves from Jericho.
literary: The chapter is built on repetition and the number seven. The LORD's instructions (verses 2-5) are repeated and carried out in detail (verses 6-16), so the reader hears the pattern again and again: priests, horns, ark, troops, rear guard, return to camp. The long description of six days of circling builds tension, and the enforced silence (verse 10) makes the final shout all the more dramatic. The climax is told quickly (verse 20). Rahab's rescue frames the destruction on both sides (verses 17, 22-25), so that the chapter's final picture is not only a burned city but a Canaanite family living among Israel to this day. The chapter ends with a verdict on Joshua that echoes God's promise in 1:5: the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land.

outline.t: The LORD's instructions for taking Jericho
The seventh day and the command of the ban
The wall falls and the city is devoted
Rahab and her family are spared
The curse on Jericho and Joshua's fame

doctrines.note: The walls fall after Israel does exactly what God says, however strange it looks. Hebrews 11:30 attributes the victory to faith, not to strategy.

Jericho's destruction is presented as God's judgment on Canaan, in keeping with Genesis 15:16, where God said the sin of the Amorites was not yet complete. The ban expresses that judgment and guards Israel from the idolatry of the land.
Inside a city under judgment, one family is saved because Rahab trusted the LORD and the spies kept their oath. Judgment and mercy stand side by side in the same chapter.
The silver, gold, bronze, and iron are holy to the LORD and belong to his treasury. What is devoted to God cannot be taken for private use, a principle that becomes the crisis of chapter 7.

words.note: Cherem, a thing devoted or the ban. It describes what is set apart irrevocably for God, either destroyed or given to the sanctuary. The same root in Arabic gives a word for a forbidden or sacred place, the source of English harem. In Joshua it is both a form of judgment on Canaanite cities and a test of Israel's obedience, since taking devoted things puts Israel itself under the ban (verse 18).

Shofar, the ram's horn trumpet. It is blown throughout the march and gives the signal for the shout. The shofar is still blown in Jewish worship on the New Year (Rosh Hashanah) and at the end of the Day of Atonement.
Rua, to shout, raise a cry. The people's shout (verses 5, 10, 16, 20) is both a battle cry and an act of worship; the same verb appears in Psalms calling people to shout for joy to the LORD.

Sheva, seven. The number appears again and again: seven priests, seven horns, seven days, and seven circuits on the seventh day. In the Bible seven is the number of completeness and of God's work, as in the seven days of creation.

christ: Hebrews 11:30-31 names both the fall of Jericho and the rescue of Rahab as acts of faith: “By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days.” The chapter's pairing of judgment and mercy anticipates the New Testament's message that God judges sin and saves those who turn to him. Rahab, spared from Jericho, becomes an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), so the one family saved from the ruined city carries the line through which the world's Savior would come. The New Testament does not treat Jericho as a model for the church's mission. Instead it takes up the language of warfare and redirects it: believers do not wage war with worldly weapons but with weapons that demolish strongholds of argument and pride (2 Corinthians 10:3-5). Revelation's seven trumpets announcing God's final judgment (Revelation 8-11) may echo the trumpets of Jericho, though the connection is thematic rather than explicit.

hard.q: How can God command the destruction of an entire city, including women and children?
hard.a: This is one of the hardest questions in the Bible, and serious readers answer it in different ways. Many interpreters emphasize that the ban was divine judgment on a culture Scripture describes as deeply corrupt, including child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), delayed for centuries until its sin was complete (Genesis 15:16), and that the God who gives life has the right to take it; they stress that it was limited to a specific time and place and never a pattern for later warfare. Others, noting that ancient Near Eastern war reports routinely used sweeping, stereotyped language of total destruction, argue that phrases like everything in the city may be hyperbole, pointing out that Joshua and Judges show many Canaanites remaining in the land (Joshua 13:1-7, 15:63, Judges 1). Some add that Jericho may have been mainly a military outpost. Still others see the text as reflecting Israel's understanding of God at a particular stage, to be read in light of the fuller revelation of God in Christ, who commands love of enemies. Many readers combine elements of these views. What the chapter itself stresses is that the ban was not for plunder, that Israel was subject to the same judgment when it sinned (chapter 7), and that even here a Canaanite family who turned to God was saved.

questions: Israel took Jericho through obedience that looked foolish. When has obedience to God seemed impractical to you, and what happened?
In the middle of a story of judgment, Rahab and her family are saved. What does that tell you about the way God's mercy works?
The silver and gold of Jericho belonged to the LORD. What in your life have you been tempted to treat as your own that really belongs to God?
